summary.text: For \(1\le n<10\), \(10n\) is an explicit partner. For \(n\ge10\), writing \(d=D(n)\), congruence modulo \(9\) makes \(L=(n+D(d-1)-D(2d-1))/9\) a nonnegative integer; digit-sum bounds ensure \(d\le10^L\), and a decimal-complement calculation gives \(D(d(2\cdot10^L-1))=9L+D(2d-1)-D(d-1)=n\), yielding a positive distinct partner since \(D(n)<n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(m)\) denote the sum of the ordinary base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(m\), with \(D(0)=0\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
It will then follow immediately that the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty. Since all its elements are positive, its least element is positive and hence \(a(n)\ne0\).

We begin with several elementary facts about decimal digit sums.

First, if \(m>0\), then \(D(m)>0\), because the decimal expansion of a positive integer has at least one nonzero digit. Also
\[
D(m)\le m.
\]
Indeed, if \(m=\sum_{i=0}^r e_i10^i\), where \(0\le e_i\le9\), then
\[
D(m)=\sum_{i=0}^r e_i\le \sum_{i=0}^r e_i10^i=m.
\]
Moreover, if \(m\ge10\), at least one nonzero digit occurs in a position \(i\ge1\), where \(10^i>1\), and therefore the preceding inequality is strict:
\[
D(m)<m\qquad(m\ge10). \tag{1}
\]

We shall also use digit-sum subadditivity:
\[
D(x+y)\le D(x)+D(y) \tag{2}
\]
for all nonnegative integers \(x,y\). Here is a proof that explicitly accounts for carries. Write
\[
x=10q_x+r_x,\qquad y=10q_y+r_y,
\]
where \(0\le r_x,r_y<10\), and put
\[
c=\left\lfloor\frac{r_x+r_y}{10}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus \(c\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). If \(r=(r_x+r_y)-10c\), then
\[
x+y=10(q_x+q_y+c)+r,
\]
and hence
\[
D(x+y)=r+D(q_x+q_y+c).
\]
An induction on \(x+y\) proves (2). The cases in which \(x=0\) or \(y=0\) are immediate. Otherwise, both \(q_x+q_y\) and \(q_x+q_y+c\) are smaller than \(x+y\), so the induction hypothesis, applied first to \(q_x+q_y\) and then to its sum with \(c\), gives
\[
D(q_x+q_y+c)
 \le D(q_x+q_y)+D(c)
 \le D(q_x)+D(q_y)+c,
\]
because \(D(c)=c\) for \(c\in\{0,1\}\). Since \(r+10c=r_x+r_y\), we have \(r+c\le r_x+r_y\). Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(x+y)
&\le r+D(q_x)+D(q_y)+c\\
&\le r_x+r_y+D(q_x)+D(q_y)\\
&=D(x)+D(y),
\end{aligned}
\]
as required.

Another standard fact is
\[
D(m)\equiv m\pmod 9. \tag{3}
\]
This follows directly from the decimal expansion, since \(10^i\equiv1\pmod9\) for every \(i\).

We next establish a bound which will ensure that a certain decimal block is long enough. For every \(n\ge10\), there is a positive integer \(S\) such that
\[
9S=n-D(n)\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(n)\le10^S. \tag{4}
\]
To see this, define the finite sum
\[
S=\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{n}{10^j}\right\rfloor,
\]
where terms are omitted once \(10^j>n\). If the decimal digits of \(n\) are \(e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_r\), then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac n{10^j}\right\rfloor
 =\sum_{i\ge j}e_i10^{i-j}.
\]
Summing first over \(j\) and then over \(i\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
9S
&=9\sum_i e_i(1+10+\cdots+10^{i-1})\\
&=\sum_i e_i(10^i-1)\\
&=n-D(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(n\ge10\), the first term \(\lfloor n/10\rfloor\) is at least \(1\), so \(S\ge1\). Also, writing \(q=\lfloor n/10\rfloor\), we have
\[
D(n)=(n\bmod10)+D(q)\le9+q\le9+S. \tag{5}
\]
For every \(S\ge1\),
\[
9+S\le10^S. \tag{6}
\]
The case \(S=1\) is equality. If it holds for \(S\), then
\(10^{S+1}=10\cdot10^S\ge10(9+S)\ge9+(S+1)\), so induction proves (6). Combining (5) and (6) gives the second part of (4).

We now record the decimal-block identity at the heart of the construction. Suppose \(d>0\) and \(d\le10^L\). Then
\[
D\bigl(d(2\cdot10^L-1)\bigr)
 =9L+D(2d-1)-D(d-1). \tag{7}
\]
Indeed,
\[
d(2\cdot10^L-1)=(2d-1)10^L+(10^L-d). \tag{8}
\]
Write \(d-1\) using exactly \(L\) decimal places, adding leading zeros if necessary. This is possible because \(d-1<10^L\). If these \(L\) digits are \(f_0,\ldots,f_{L-1}\), then
\[
10^L-d=(10^L-1)-(d-1)

a
\]
has, with exactly \(L\) places, the digits \(9-f_0,\ldots,9-f_{L-1}\). There is no borrowing because \(10^L-1\) consists of \(L\) nines. Therefore
\[
D(10^L-d)=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}(9-f_i)=9L-D(d-1). \tag{9}
\]
Equation (8) concatenates the decimal expansion of \(2d-1\) with this lower block of exactly \(L\) places. Hence digit sums add across the two blocks. Using (9) gives (7).

We now construct a partner for an arbitrary \(n\ge10\). Set
\[
d=D(n),\qquad A=D(d-1),\qquad B=D(2d-1).
\]
Since \(n>0\), we have \(d>0\). By (2), the identity
\[
2d-1=(d-1)+d
\]
gives
\[
B=D((d-1)+d)\le D(d-1)+D(d)\le A+d. \tag{10}
\]
Since \(d=D(n)\le n\), this also shows \(B\le A+n\).

By (3),
\[
n\equiv d,\qquad A\equiv d-1,\qquad B\equiv2d-1\pmod9.
\]
As \(d>0\), \(d+(d-1)=2d-1\), so these congruences imply
\[
n+A-B\equiv0\pmod9.
\]
The quantity \(n+A-B\) is nonnegative by (10). Thus there is a nonnegative integer \(L\) satisfying
\[
n+A=9L+B. \tag{11}
\]

We must verify that this \(L\) is large enough to apply (7). Choose \(S\) as in (4). From (10) and (11),
\[
9L=n+A-B\ge n-d.
\]
But (4), with \(d=D(n)\), says \(n-d=9S\). Hence \(L\ge S\). Again by (4),
\[
d\le10^S\le10^L. \tag{12}
\]

Define
\[
k=d(2\cdot10^L-1).
\]
It is positive: \(d>0\), and \(2\cdot10^L-1>0\). Plainly \(d\mid k\). By (7), (11), and the definitions of \(A,B\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(k)
 &=9L+B-A\\
 &=n. \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
D(n)=d\mid k
\]
and, because \(D(k)=n\),
\[
D(k)\mid n.
\]
It remains only to check that the constructed partner differs from \(n\). If \(k=n\), then (13) would give
\[
n=D(k)=D(n)=d,
\]
contradicting the strict inequality \(D(n)<n\) from (1), since \(n\ge10\). Therefore \(k\ne n\), and \(k\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\).

Finally consider the positive integers below \(10\). If \(1\le n\le9\), take
\[
k=10n.
\]
Then \(D(n)=n\) and \(D(10n)=n\). Therefore \(D(n)\mid k\) and \(D(k)\mid n\). Moreover, \(k>0\) and \(k\ne n\). Thus these integers also have Harshad amicable partners.

We have now shown that for every positive integer \(n\), the set
\[
\{k>0:k\ne n,\ D(n)\mid k,\ D(k)\mid n\}
\]
is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least element, and that element is positive. This least element is precisely \(a(n)\) under the stated definition of the sequence. Consequently \(a(n)\ne0\) for every positive integer \(n\), proving the conjecture.
